props.title: Baba Yaga

sections.content: **Baba Yaga (1973)** (1973) stands as a fascinating fusion of European comic book aesthetics and Italian giallo sensibilities. Based on Guido Crepax's erotic comic "Valentina," director Corrado Farina crafts a psychedelic journey through supernatural horror and mod fashion. The film follows photographer Valentina Rosselli (Isabelle De Funès) after her encounter with the mysterious Baba Yaga (Carroll Baker), a witch who curses her camera and unleashes a series of surreal, erotically-charged events. It shares DNA with contemporary Italian horror classics like **Deep Red** (1975) and **All the Colors of the Dark** (1972) in its blend of style, sexuality, and supernatural elements.

sections.content: The 1970s marked a golden age for occult cinema blending eroticism with supernatural horror. Films like **The Devil's Daughter** (1973) and Lisa and the Devil (1973) tapped into similar territory as Baba Yaga, exploring feminine power through a lens of mysticism and sexuality. Jean Rollin's **Lips of Blood** (1975) and **Fascination** (1979) created their own distinct erotic-horror vocabulary in France, while Italy produced **The Perfume of the Lady in Black** (1974) and **All the Colors of the Dark** (1972). SUBHEAD: Comic Book Connection and Visual Innovation

Baba Yaga's comic book origins make it a unique entry in 1970s European horror. While most comic adaptations of the era focused on superheroes or sword-and-sorcery, Farina embraced Crepax's avant-garde storytelling and erotic surrealism. The film's innovative visual techniques, including split-screens and photo-montages, influenced later comic adaptations like **Diabolik** (1968) and **Danger: Diabolik** (1968). These techniques would later be refined by directors like Brian De Palma in films such as **Sisters** (1972) and **Phantom of the Paradise** (1974).
